title: Hobbies, Preferences & Natural Small Talk
subtitle: A manageable lesson on unusual hobbies, precise preference language and useful verb–preposition partnerships.

teacherNote.summary: The approved original platform design is preserved. Workload is manageable, all learner-facing explanations are English, and the final unrelated French-word discussion is excluded.

lessonNotes: Small talk becomes more natural when you react to one detail and ask a connected follow-up question.
Unusual hobbies are useful conversation topics because they invite genuine questions and memorable vocabulary.
Preference phrases have different strengths. Choosing the right one makes an opinion sound more precise and natural.

grammar.title: Strong and moderate preferences
grammar.rule: Use be crazy about or love for strong enthusiasm. Use really like for a clear positive feeling and quite like for a milder, more measured preference.

grammar.title: Neutral and negative preferences
grammar.rule: Use don’t mind when something is acceptable but not especially exciting. Use can’t stand or hate for strong dislike.
examples: Felix hates waiting in long queues.

grammar.title: Verb–preposition partnerships
grammar.rule: Learn the verb and its preposition as one unit: listen to, look at, come up to, wait for, spend time on, and talk to or with somebody.
examples: A visitor came up to Marco.
Ravi spends time on his collection.

remember: Preference language works like a scale: be crazy about / love → really like → quite like → don’t mind → can’t stand / hate.
watchOut: Really like is normally stronger than quite like. Also remember the complete partnership: listen to something, wait for someone and spend time on something.

conversation.q: Maya: “I collect old concert tickets.” What is the best reply?
opt: That sounds interesting. Which ticket is your favourite?
conversation.a: That sounds interesting. Which ticket is your favourite?
conversation.why: React first, then ask a connected question.

conversation.q: Leo: “I’m crazy about birdwatching.” Choose the natural response.
opt: How did you become interested in it?
conversation.a: How did you become interested in it?
conversation.why: This follow-up invites a personal story.

conversation.q: Nora: “I quite like photography.” What does she mean?
opt: She has never heard of it.
conversation.why: Quite like is positive but not very strong.

conversation.q: Arda: “I can’t stand waiting in queues.” Choose the best reaction.
opt: Neither can I. They can be exhausting.
conversation.a: Neither can I. They can be exhausting.
conversation.why: A short reaction keeps the conversation natural.

conversation.q: Tara: “I’ve started collecting postcards.” Choose the best next question.
conversation.why: Ask for a practical detail linked to the hobby.

reading.title: Two Hobbies, One Good Conversation
reading.text:
At a community exhibition, Nora stopped beside a table covered with old coins, postcards and small labels. The display belonged to Tomas, a quiet collector who had studied numismatics for several years. Nora knew almost nothing about coins, but one object caught her attention: a dark silver coin from the early twentieth century. Instead of pretending to understand it, she asked a simple follow-up question: “How did you find this one?”

Tomas explained that he had discovered it in a box at a local market. He really liked researching the stories behind ordinary objects. The financial value was not the most important part for him. He spent time on old maps, newspaper archives and family records because each source added another piece to the coin’s journey. Nora listened to his explanation and realised that collecting could be a form of historical detective work.

A few minutes later, Tomas noticed the camera around Nora’s neck. She was crazy about street photography and often walked through unfamiliar neighbourhoods at weekends. She loved capturing small moments that other people passed without noticing: reflections in shop windows, unusual signs or strangers laughing at a bus stop. However, she could not stand taking carefully arranged studio photographs. They felt too controlled for her.

The conversation worked because neither person gave a long lecture. Tomas explained one memorable coin and then asked about the camera. Nora described one type of photograph and showed him a recent image. They reacted to each other’s details and asked natural questions. By the end of the conversation, Nora quite liked the idea of visiting a coin market, while Tomas wanted to try a short photography walk.

Their interests remained different, but the exchange showed that a hobby does not need to be shared before it becomes an interesting topic. Curiosity, a specific example and one good follow-up question can create a meaningful conversation between two people who have just met.

questions.q: Why does Nora ask about the silver coin?
opt: She wants to sell her camera.
questions.why: The first paragraph identifies the object that starts the conversation.
He treats collecting as historical detective work.

questions.q: What kind of photography does Nora dislike?
questions.why: She feels that studio photographs are too controlled.

questions.q: Why does the conversation work well?
opt: They give specific examples and ask connected questions.
questions.a: They give specific examples and ask connected questions.
questions.why: The final paragraphs explain the conversation strategy.

questions.q: What does Nora think by the end?
opt: She might visit a coin market.
She wants to stop taking photographs.
questions.a: She might visit a coin market.
questions.why: Quite like shows a new, moderate interest.

opt: Curiosity can connect people with different interests.
questions.a: Curiosity can connect people with different interests.
questions.why: The conclusion connects hobby differences with successful small talk.

questions.q: In the text, “source” most nearly means…
questions.why: Maps, archives and records provide information.

questions.q: Which phrase describes Nora’s strongest preference?
opt: She was crazy about street photography.
questions.a: She was crazy about street photography.
questions.why: Be crazy about is the strongest positive phrase shown.

listening.title: Love It or Hate It — Free-time Activities
listening.source: ELLLO English Listening Lesson Library Online
listening.instructions: Listen once for the activities and overall opinions. Listen again and note the exact language used to express likes and dislikes. Use the transcript only after two listening attempts.

questions.q: What should you note on the second listen?
questions.why: The lesson focus is preference strength.
It means the activity is acceptable.

questions.q: When should you use the transcript?
questions.why: The transcript is for final checking.

writing.prompt: Write 70–100 words about a fictional person with an interesting hobby. Describe the hobby, explain the strength of the person’s preference, use at least two verb–preposition partnerships and finish with one natural follow-up question.
